cards.title: Kitchen oil fires
facts: Water on burning oil turns instantly to steam and throws burning oil into the air (a fireball).
Fire needs heat, fuel and oxygen. Covering the pan cuts off oxygen.
A covered pan should stay covered until it has completely cooled.
do: Turn off the stove or gas if you can reach it safely
Slide a metal lid or baking tray over the pan
Use a damp (wrung-out) towel if there is no lid
Get everyone out, close the kitchen door and call 101 or 112 if the fire spreads
dont: Never pour water on burning oil
Don't carry the burning pan outside
Don't throw flour on it, it can flare up

myths.statement: Water can put out any kind of fire.
myths.truth: Water makes oil and electrical fires much worse. Smother oil fires, and cut the power for electrical ones.

myths.statement: Covering a burning pan with a metal lid can put the fire out.
myths.truth: A lid cuts off oxygen. Keep it on until the pan cools down.

quiz.q: Oil in a pan catches fire. What's the safest first move?
options: Cover it with a metal lid
quiz.explanation: A lid cuts off oxygen. Water causes a dangerous fireball.

quiz.q: After covering a burning pan, when can you lift the lid?
options: Only when the pan has fully cooled
quiz.explanation: Lifting it early lets oxygen back in, and hot oil can reignite.

situations: It's {time}. {name} is frying snacks when the oil in the pan suddenly catches fire. Flames reach up toward the chimney hood, and {relation} runs in with a mug of water.
{name} is helping make pakoras {at}. The oil overheats and bursts into flames. Someone shouts 'Get water!'
scenario.question: What should {name} do, right now?

rubric.note: Water on burning oil causes a fireball.
Switching off the gas stops the fire getting fuel.

rubric.point: Cover the pan with a metal lid or damp cloth
rubric.note: Covering it cuts off oxygen. The fastest way to put out a small oil fire.

rubric.point: Get out and call for help if it spreads
rubric.note: Leave, close the door, call 101 (fire) or 112.

cards.title: Getting out of a building fire
facts: Smoke rises, so the cleanest air is near the floor.
Lifts can stop or open onto a smoky floor during a fire.
Closed doors slow down fire and smoke.
do: Shout 'Fire!' to warn others
Use the stairs, never the lift
Stay low under smoke
Feel doors with the back of your hand before opening
Close doors behind you
Go to the assembly point and stay there
Call 101 or 112 once you're safe

myths.statement: If there's a fire in your building, take the lift. It's the fastest way out.
myths.truth: Lifts can stop working or open onto a smoky floor. Always use the stairs.

myths.statement: In a smoky room, crawling low helps you breathe cleaner air.
myths.truth: Smoke and heat rise, so the air near the floor is cleaner.

quiz.q: The fire alarm rings in your apartment building. How do you go down?
options: Go up to the roof first
quiz.explanation: Stairs are the safe way out. Lifts can fail in a fire.

quiz.q: Before opening a door during a fire, you should…
options: Feel it with the back of your hand
quiz.explanation: A hot door means fire on the other side. Use another way out.

situations: {name} is {at}, on the 6th floor, when the fire alarm goes off and the corridor starts filling with grey smoke. {relation} heads straight for the lift.
It's {time}. {name} smells smoke and hears the alarm {at}. The door to the stairwell is closed, and people are shouting.
scenario.question: What should {name} do to get out safely?

rubric.point: Use the stairs, not the lift
rubric.note: Lifts can stop or open onto a smoky floor.
Cleaner air is near the floor.

rubric.point: Check doors for heat and close doors behind
rubric.note: Hot door = fire behind it. Closed doors slow the fire.

rubric.point: Get out, go to the assembly point, call 101/112

cards.title: Electrical fires and sockets
facts: Water conducts electricity, so it can cause electric shock on an electrical fire.
Overloaded sockets and damaged wires are a common cause of home fires.
Dry powder (ABC) or CO2 extinguishers are suitable for electrical fires.
do: Switch off power at the main switch if it's safe
Tell an adult immediately
Get out and call 101 or 112 if it grows
Report burning smells and sparking sockets
dont: Never throw water on an electrical fire
Don't plug many heavy appliances into one socket

myths.statement: It's fine to use water on a burning TV as long as you're quick.
myths.truth: Water conducts electricity. Cut the power first and use the right extinguisher, or get out.

quiz.q: A phone charger starts sparking and smoking. First step?
options: Switch off the power if safe and tell an adult
Pull the wire with wet hands
quiz.explanation: Cutting the power removes the danger. Never use water.

situations: {name} is studying {at} when the extension board under the desk starts sparking and a thin line of smoke rises. {relation} grabs a bottle of water.
scenario.question: What should {name} do?

rubric.point: Don't use water on an electrical fire
Switch off power at the main switch if safe
Tell an adult and get out / call 101 or 112 if it grows
Use a suitable extinguisher only if trained
rubric.note: ABC dry powder or CO2 are suitable for electrical fires.

cards.title: Diyas and firecrackers
facts: Most festival burns happen to hands, face and eyes.
Synthetic clothes can melt onto skin; cotton is safer.
A cracker that didn't go off can still explode later.
do: Only use crackers with an adult watching
Keep a bucket of water and sand nearby
Light at arm's length and step back
Wear cotton clothes and closed shoes
Keep diyas away from curtains and loose clothes
dont: Never relight a cracker that didn't go off
Don't hold crackers in your hand
Don't burst crackers indoors or near vehicles

myths.statement: If a cracker doesn't go off, it's safe to walk up and light it again.
myths.truth: A dud can explode without warning. Wait, then soak it in water.

quiz.q: What should be kept nearby when bursting crackers?
options: A bucket of water and sand
quiz.explanation: Water and sand help with small fires and duds.

situations: It's Diwali night. {At}, a cracker {name} lit doesn't go off. {relation} says 'Go check it and light it again!'
scenario.question: What should {name} do?

rubric.point: Don't go near or relight the dud
Wait, then soak it in a bucket of water
Make sure an adult is supervising
